summary: Defines the List-Id email header, which gives each mailing list a unique, stable identifier. Mail software can use it to reliably recognize messages from a particular list, regardless of the list's address.

eli5.summary: Every mailing list gets a name tag stamped on its messages so your email program can sort them correctly.

questions: how to identify mailing list messages
how long can a list-id be
subtitle: A mail header that gives each mailing list a stable, domain-based identifier.

tldr.problem: Mail software needs to recognize which mailing list a message belongs to, but the list's submission address can change when its host, software or policy changes.
tldr.mechanism: The List-Id header carries a list identifier of the form list-label.namespace, where the namespace is a domain the list owner controls, or the special unmanaged namespace localhost.
tldr.outcome: Filters and mail clients can match on a persistent identifier independent of the delivering host, although it must not be treated as proof that a message is authentic.

today: RFC 2919 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to the list command headers of RFC 2369.

sections.title: Why Lists Need an Identifier
sections.content:
Proposals like RFC 2369 let mail user agents (MUAs) offer more list functions, but doing so depends on accurately identifying which list a message belongs to. The obvious candidate, the list's submission address, can change when the list server host, the list software or the submission policy changes. That makes automated processing and filtering hard.

A unique identifier can be used for simple string matching in a filter, to identify messages independent of the delivering host, or as a key into a database of mailing lists.
sections.eli5: A list's mailbox address can change, like moving house. A name tag that stays the same lets your email program still know whose mail it is.

sections.title: The List Identifier Syntax
sections.content:
A list identifier normally looks like a host name in a domain of the list owner. Only the rights-holder of a domain or subdomain may create identifiers in its namespace, and an owner MUST NOT generate identifiers in a domain for which they have no authority. The ABNF is list-id = list-label "." list-id-namespace, where the label is dot-atom-text and the namespace is either a domain name or the unmanaged namespace localhost.

People who do not control a domain, such as personal users, may use the reserved name localhost (see RFC 2606). A list-id MUST NOT be longer than 255 octets, for future compatibility.
sections.eli5: Names are built like web addresses, and only the owner of an address may hand out names under it. People without one use a special do-it-yourself ending.

sections.title: The List-Id Header Field
sections.content:
The header SHOULD be on all messages distributed by the list, including command responses to individual users, and on other messages that clearly apply to the list. At most one may be present, and it MUST only be generated by mailing list software, not end users.

The identifier sits in angle brackets, with an optional descriptive phrase before it: list-id-header = "List-ID:" [phrase] "<" list-id ">" CRLF. MTAs MUST NOT insert whitespace within the brackets, and clients should ignore any that appears. Unlike most RFC 822 headers, this one does not allow free whitespace and comments around tokens. For many MUAs, parsing is just extracting the text between the brackets.
sections.eli5: The tag goes inside angle brackets, and a friendly name may sit in front of it. Only the list's own software may stick it on.

sections.title: Persistence and Uniqueness
sections.content:
An administrator MAY change the identifier, but should avoid it, even when the host changes, because an MUA SHOULD treat a different identifier as a different list. Changing the description has no such disadvantage. Moving from the unmanaged namespace to a domain namespace is an acceptable reason to change it, and so is a sufficiently changed focus for the list.

Identifiers not ending in .localhost MUST be globally unique. Placing them under a list-id subdomain is suggested, for example list-id.within.com. Identifiers ending in .localhost are not guaranteed unique. They SHOULD include the creation month and year as MMYYYY and MUST include a random string, preferably a hex encoding of 128 bits of randomness (32 hex characters).
sections.eli5: Once a list has its name tag, it should keep it. Names under a real address are never shared, while do-it-yourself names add a long random jumble to make a clash unlikely.

sections.title: Comparison and Nested Lists
sections.content:
The only defined operation is case-insensitive equality. The comparison MUST ignore everything outside the angle brackets, and the MUA MAY tell the user if the descriptive name changes.

A sublist in a nested hierarchy MUST NOT modify the List-Id field. If a list processor meets a List-Id from an unexpected source, it SHOULD NOT pass it through to the list. This implies that list processors may need updating to support nested lists.
sections.eli5: Two tags match if the letters are the same, big or small. Only the part inside the brackets counts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC sees few new security concerns. Forged headers are a problem inherent in Internet email, and the implications here are relatively harmless. List processors SHOULD NOT let user-originated List-Id fields pass through to their lists, since they could confuse users and create security problems.

On the client side, a forged identifier may break automated processing. The list identifier SHOULD NOT be used as an indication that a message is authentic.
sections.eli5: Anyone could write a fake name tag, so a tag alone does not prove who sent a message.
